fields.Front: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array by index?
fields.Back: O(1) — arrays support direct address calculation (base + index * elementSize).

fields.Front: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the head of a singly linked list?
fields.Back: O(1) — you just repoint the head pointer, no shifting required.

fields.Front: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list by index?
fields.Back: O(n) — there is no random access; you must traverse node-by-node from the head.

fields.Front: What is the time and space complexity of push/pop on an array-backed stack of n elements?
fields.Back: Time: O(1) per operation (amortized, due to occasional resizing). Space: O(n) total for the stack's contents.

fields.Front: What is the average-case time complexity of lookup, insert, and delete on a hash table?
fields.Back: O(1) average case — the hash function maps keys to buckets directly.

fields.Front: What is the worst-case time complexity of a hash table lookup, and what causes it?
fields.Back: O(n) — happens when many keys collide into the same bucket (e.g. a poor hash function), degrading a bucket into a linear list/chain.

fields.Front: What are the two main strategies for resolving hash collisions?
fields.Back:
Chaining — each bucket holds a linked list (or tree) of colliding entries.
Open addressing — on collision, probe for another empty slot in the table itself (e.g. linear/quadratic probing, double hashing).

fields.Front: What is the time complexity of search, insert, and delete on a balanced binary search tree vs. a degenerate/unbalanced one (e.g. sorted-order inserts with no rebalancing)?
fields.Back:
Balanced: O(log n) — height stays ~log n.
Degenerate: O(n) — the tree collapses into a linked list.

fields.Front: What is the time complexity of inserting into, or extracting the min/max from, a binary heap of n elements?
fields.Back: O(log n) — the new/last element sifts up or down at most the height of the tree.

fields.Front: What underlying data structure does BFS use to visit nodes, and what does DFS use?
fields.Back: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to explore level by level. DFS uses a stack (explicit, or the call stack via recursion) to explore one branch fully before backtracking.

fields.Front: In an unweighted graph, which traversal (BFS or DFS) is guaranteed to find the shortest path between two nodes?
fields.Back: BFS — it explores nodes in increasing distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest path.

fields.Front: What is the time and space complexity of BFS/DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges (adjacency list)?
fields.Back: Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) for the visited set plus the queue/stack/recursion depth.

fields.Front: What precondition does binary search require on its input, and what is its time complexity?
fields.Back: The array must be sorted. Time complexity: O(log n) — each comparison halves the search space.

fields.Front: What is quicksort's average-case and worst-case time complexity, and is it stable?
fields.Back: Average: O(n log n). Worst case: O(n²) (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive pivot choice). Not stable by default (equal elements can be reordered during partitioning).

fields.Front: What is merge sort's time complexity (best/avg/worst) and space complexity, and is it stable?
fields.Back: Time: O(n log n) in all cases (always splits and merges the full input). Space: O(n) for the merge buffers. Stable — equal elements keep their relative order.

fields.Front: What is heap sort's time and space complexity, and is it stable?
fields.Back: Time: O(n log n) in all cases. Space: O(1) extra (sorts in place). Not stable — swaps during heapify can reorder equal elements.

fields.Front: In terms of memory, what is the main tradeoff of writing an algorithm recursively instead of iteratively?
fields.Back: Recursion consumes O(depth) extra space on the call stack for pending stack frames; a well-written iterative version can often do the same work in O(1) extra space.

fields.Front: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?
fields.Back: Overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur) and optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems).

fields.Front: Stack
fields.Back: A LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) data structure supporting push and pop from the same end.

fields.Front: Queue
fields.Back: A FIFO (First-In, First-Out) data structure supporting enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front.

fields.Text: Big-O notation describes the {{c1::upper bound}} (worst-case growth rate) of an algorithm's time or space requirements as input size n grows.

In a {{c1::min-heap}}, every parent node is less than or equal to its children (root is the minimum); in a {{c2::max-heap}}, every parent is greater than or equal to its children (root is the maximum).
fields.Extra: A heap is a complete binary tree, usually array-backed.
